comm-1.prompt: Turn each blaming line into an “I feel” line.
comm-1.why: Starting with your feeling, not their fault, lets the other person hear the problem instead of defending themselves.

cards.text: “You clearly don’t want to see me.”
Deciding they’re angry from a short text
“I noticed you’ve been quiet. What’s up?”
“I know exactly why you did that.”

comm-2.why: Assumptions fill the gaps with your worst guess; a gentle question gets you the real story instead.

comm-3.prompt: Raising a tricky topic. Put these in order.
items: Ask if now is a good time
Agree a time if it isn’t
comm-3.why: Checking the timing first means they can actually listen; one gentle point at a time keeps it from snowballing.

lines.text: My flatmate ate my leftovers AGAIN.
And I said nothing. I feel like such a pushover 😩

options.text: Just label your food, problem solved!
options.reaction: Yeah… that’s not really the point though.
options.why: Jumping to a fix skips the feeling they shared, so they don’t feel heard.

options.text: So it’s not just the food, it’s feeling like you can’t speak up?
options.reaction: Exactly that. I always just swallow it.
options.why: Reflecting the deeper feeling shows you were listening and helps them open up more.

options.text: Ugh, my old flatmate was way worse.
options.why: Switching to your story takes the spotlight off them just when they needed it.

comm-5.prompt: Match each slip with a quick repair.

pairs.b: “Sorry, go on. I cut you off.”

comm-5.why: Repairs work best when they’re quick and small. Naming the slip lightly stops it from turning into a bigger fight.

trust-1.prompt: A promise you can keep, or a risky one?

cards.text: “I’ll check and let you know by Friday.”

trust-1.why: Small, specific promises are easy to keep, and every one you keep adds to trust; sweeping ones are bound to slip.

trust-2.prompt: Match each non-apology with a real one.
trust-2.why: A real apology owns your action plainly; “if”, “but” and vague wording all quietly shift the blame away.

trust-3.title: An off morning

lines.text: You okay? You seemed really off this morning.

trust-3.prompt: You were stressed about work. Reply:

options.text: Sorry! Just stressed about a deadline, nothing you did. I’ll be better company tonight 💛
options.reaction: Phew, okay. Good luck with it! 💛
options.why: Explaining your mood means they don’t have to guess, which is exactly what makes you feel safe to be around.

options.text: I’m fine.
options.why: A short “fine” leaves them guessing and often worrying it was about them.

options.text: Why does everything have to be about you?
options.reaction: Wow, I was just checking in.
options.why: Taking the stress out on them makes your moods feel unpredictable and unsafe.

trust-4.prompt: Rebuilding trust. Put these in order.
trust-4.why: The apology opens the door, but it’s openness, patience and repeated proof over time that actually rebuild trust.

bound-1.prompt: Within your limits, or past them?

cards.text: Saying yes and feeling fine about it
Agreeing, then resenting it all week
Helping and still having energy left
Cancelling your own plans yet again
Dreading their name on your phone

bound-1.why: Resentment, dread and always putting yourself last are signs you’ve gone past a limit and need to set one.

bound-2.title: Can I borrow it?

lines.text: Can I borrow your car this weekend? 🙏

bound-2.prompt: You don’t lend your car. Reply:

options.text: Umm, maybe? Let me think about it…
options.reaction: Great, I’ll pick up the keys Friday! 😄
options.why: A soft maybe often gets heard as a yes, and then saying no gets harder.

options.text: Sorry, I just can’t, I’ve got so much on and the insurance and…
options.reaction: What if I paid for petrol?
options.why: Long excuses invite bargaining, because they sound like problems to be solved.

options.text: I don’t lend my car, but I could drop you at the station on Saturday?
options.reaction: Fair enough! A lift would be great, thanks 😊
options.why: A clear, warm no with something you can offer keeps both the boundary and the friendship.

bound-3.title: A late-night message

lines.text: I really need to vent about my boss

bound-3.prompt: It’s 1am, and you asked them not to call this late. Reply:

options.text: Sure, call me.
options.why: Giving in teaches them the boundary doesn’t really count, and you’ll be exhausted tomorrow.

options.text: I care, and I want to hear it. I’m off to sleep now though. Lunch tomorrow?
options.reaction: Sorry, forgot the time! Lunch is perfect 💛
options.why: You repeat the boundary calmly and kindly, and offer a time that works, so they still feel cared for.

options.text: Seriously?! I literally told you not to do this.
options.why: Holding the line is right, but the sharp tone turns it into a fight.

bound-4.prompt: Respecting their no, or pushing it?
bound-4.why: Respecting a no means taking it the first time, without guilt-tripping or trying to wear them down.

conf-1.prompt: Match each heated line with a cooler one.
conf-1.why: Cooler words describe the problem or ask for a pause instead of attacking, which keeps the argument from boiling over.

conf-2.prompt: Same team, or against each other?

cards.text: “What would work for both of us?”
Keeping score of who did what
“Shall we try a rota for a week?”

conf-2.why: When you tackle the problem together instead of each other, you find solutions much faster.

cards.text: Bringing up something from last year

conf-3.why: Fair fights stay on one issue and keep respect; foul moves win the moment but damage the relationship.

conf-4.prompt: Finding a compromise. Put these in order.
items: Say what matters most to you
Ask what matters most to them
conf-4.why: Knowing what really matters to each of you shows where you can bend and where you can’t, so nobody loses.

conn-1.title: A small moment

lines.text: omg the dog just stole an ENTIRE sandwich off my plate 😭
I looked away for two seconds

conn-1.prompt: You’re busy, but you have ten seconds. Reply:

options.text: lol
options.why: It’s a reply, but it doesn’t really turn towards the moment they wanted to share.

options.text: (You’ll reply later.)
options.why: Small bids like this are easy to miss, but missing lots of them slowly builds distance.

options.text: NO 😂 the whole thing?? Send me a pic of the guilty face
options.why: Ten seconds of real interest turns a tiny bid into a shared moment, which is how closeness grows.

conn-2.prompt: Match each closed question with a deeper one.

pairs.b: “What was the best bit of today?”

conn-2.why: Open, specific questions invite stories and feelings, not just a one-word answer, so the talk can go deeper.

conn-3.prompt: Starting a ritual. Put these in order.
conn-3.why: Small rituals at a set time are easy to start and hard to drop, which is exactly what keeps people close.

conn-4.title: A favour at work

lines.text: Btw I fixed the formulas in your spreadsheet 🙂
They were all pointing at the old tab

conn-4.prompt: It saved you hours before a deadline. Reply:

options.text: thx
options.why: A quick thanks is polite, but it doesn’t show her what the help really meant.

options.text: You legend! That saved me hours before Friday’s deadline. Thank you 🙌
options.why: Specific thanks, naming what she did and why it mattered, is the kind people remember.

options.text: Oh, I was going to get round to that.
options.why: Brushing it off can make kindness feel unwelcome, so it’s less likely to happen again.

list-1.prompt: Giving full attention. Put these in order.
list-1.why: Clearing distractions and facing them shows you’re there; letting them finish and following up proves it.

lines.text: I don’t know. I just feel stuck in my job.
Everyone else seems to be moving on with their lives.

options.text: Sounds like you’re feeling left behind while others move forward. Is that it?
options.reaction: Yeah… that’s exactly it. It’s been eating at me.
options.why: You put their feeling into words and checked it, which helps them feel understood and say more.

options.text: You should update your CV this weekend!
options.why: Advice can wait. First they need to feel you’ve understood what they’re going through.

options.text: Everyone feels like that sometimes.
options.why: It’s meant kindly, but it shrinks their feeling instead of reflecting it.

list-3.prompt: Match each feeling with a validating reply.
list-3.why: Validating says the feeling makes sense. You don’t have to agree or fix anything for it to help.

cards.text: “Do you want advice, or just to vent?”
Staying with them while they talk

list-4.why: Often people need to feel supported before they want solutions, so asking what they need is a good start.
